title: SoFi Built a Balance Sheet Bank While Selling a Capital-Light Story
subtitle: The October 27 print will show whether fee income can salvage fintech multiples.
summary: SoFi pitched investors on a frictionless platform that would originate loans and pass the risk to third parties, but rapid balance-sheet expansion turned it back into a traditional lender. Re-rating the equity now requires proving that originations can actually leave the building without crushing margins.

bodyHtml:
Think of SoFi like an airline that promised Wall Street it would make all its money selling high-margin frequent flier miles. Then it spent the year buying jet fuel and parking airplanes on the tarmac. At its core, the company is a digital consumer bank. You download the app to manage your checking account, buy fractional shares, or refinance your student loans, and SoFi turns around and lends your deposits out as personal debt and mortgages.

The Numbers That Matter
Price LIVE$14.90
Market Cap$19.2B
Forward P/E18.1
Total Revenue (TTM)$4.27B
52-Week Low$13.86
52-Week High$32.73
Analyst ConsensusHold (23 analysts)
Analyst Target Mean$20.36
Price refreshes live. All other figures as of October 21, 2026.

Most startup neobanks rent their regulatory plumbing from partner institutions because getting approved by banking regulators takes years. SoFi did the hard work and bought a national bank charter, which gives it an enormous advantage. It funds loans with everyday customer deposits rather than expensive corporate credit lines, saving an annualized $712.6 million versus what warehouse funding would have cost.

That funding advantage is real, but it masks a strategic bait-and-switch that Wall Street is finally pricing in. A dollar of pure fee income arrives without strings attached, meaning a company can reinvest it immediately into software or return it to investors. A dollar of lending income, by contrast, forces a bank to lock up regulatory capital against the asset in case the borrower stumbles.

SoFi earned a tech multiple because management pitched a capital-light future where it would originate loans and immediately hand them off to institutional buyers for upfront fees. In 2026, the exact opposite happened. Fee-based revenue fell from 43% of total top-line revenue late last year to 39% by the second quarter. Meanwhile, its dedicated Loan Platform Business slid 26% in revenue from its peak, shrinking to less than 12% of total net revenue.

When institutional buyers got cold feet, SoFi chose to absorb the volume rather than slow down origination growth. Of the $10.7 billion in personal loans originated in the second quarter, $7.6 billion stayed parked right on SoFi’s own ledger. Total assets jumped 48% year-over-year to $60.95 billion, pulling net interest income up 52% while non-interest income grew just 21%.

The software side of the house failed to pick up the slack. Revenue across its B2B tech platforms dropped 23% year-over-year after a major enterprise customer departed, leaving contribution margin in that segment at just 14%. Even SoFi's artificial intelligence rollouts—including its conversational financial guide and automated document review tools—are customer-service helpers designed to trim operational overhead rather than algorithmic underwriting moats that reduce credit risk.

The bear case is not that personal loan borrowers are defaulting en masse. Net charge-offs actually dropped to 2.62% in the second quarter, proving that consumer credit health is holding up. The real short thesis is that SoFi is an ordinary balance-sheet bank masquerading in an expensive software costume.

Net interest income is carrying the growth, and seven out of every ten personal loan dollars land on the company's own balance sheet. Keefe, Bruyette & Woods estimates that interest-rate shifts created a headwind exceeding $1.0 billion before hedging. An expected $825 million in adjusted net income works out to an 8.7% return on tangible common equity. For a plain balance-sheet lender, roughly 18 times forward earnings is still a rich price. Bears win if charge-offs climb back over 3.0%, loan platform revenue drops below $140 million, or management leaves full-year earnings guidance frozen for a fourth straight report.

For the stock to break its downward spiral and trade like a premium platform again, the origination mix has to change. Fee revenue needs to claw its way back toward 45% of total sales, and the Loan Platform Business has to climb past its prior high of $193.7 million. Management also needs to prove operating leverage by raising full-year earnings guidance beyond the current $0.60 per share, ending a pattern where revenue beats produced zero bottom-line revisions.

That test arrives before the opening bell on October 27. Wall Street consensus expects roughly $1.257 billion in revenue and about $0.166 in per-share profit, with analyst sentiment pinned at Hold. The headline numbers will matter less than where the loans actually ended up.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in SOFI. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
